scenario: WIBTA if I told my cousin his kid can’t stay in our house? | My cousin (M27) recently moved in with my husband and I. We completely closed of the very large main bedroom and bathroom to create a flatlet for him that’s separate from the house with his own entrance so it’s basically two separate units of one house. Now my cousin has a 2 year old and he’s busy with a custody battle with his ex so he can get to spend more time with his son. I completely support this and really hopes he gets more time with his son. Yesterday my cousin came to ask me if it would be possible for my husband and I to convert our spare bedroom into a room for his son if and when he comes to visit over weekends. There is no access from my cousin’s room into our part of the house and he doesn’t have keys to come and go as he pleases. I understand that the court will be looking into his living situation to see if he has suitable space for his son to stay with him (and to be honest his current room and bathroom is more than big enough) but I’m not comfortable with letting his son sleep in our house if my cousin has no access to him and I’m not willing to take responsibility for his kid. The whole family is involved in this because that’s just the way my family is and everyone expects me to help out my cousin with his current custody situation to get him more time with his son. WIBTA for telling him I will not allow his son to sleep in our house and completely jeopardizing his court case?

First, the user has a cousin who recently moved in with her and her husband. They've set up a separate flatlet for him, which is completely closed off from the main house. This means the cousin has his own entrance and no access to the rest of the house. The user supports her cousin in his custody battle with his ex, hoping he gets more time with his son.

Now, the cousin is asking if they can convert their spare bedroom into a room for his son during weekend visits. The user isn't comfortable with this because the cousin doesn't have access to the spare bedroom and she doesn't want to take responsibility for the child. The family is involved, and everyone expects her to help her cousin, which could jeopardize his court case if she says no.

So, the question is: Is it morally acceptable for her to tell her cousin no, potentially harming his custody case?

I think about the factors involved. On one hand, the user has a right to set boundaries regarding who stays in her house and under what conditions. She doesn't feel comfortable having the child there without the cousin having access, which makes sense from a safety and responsibility standpoint.

On the other hand, her cousin is in a difficult situation fighting for custody, and her refusal could impact his case. The court might look at his living situation to determine if he has a suitable space for his son. If the user refuses to allow the child to stay, it might seem like she's not supporting him, which could be interpreted negatively by the court.

But wait, the user already has a separate flatlet for the cousin, which is more than enough space for the son. So, maybe the court wouldn't require the child to stay in the main house. The user's main concern is not wanting to take responsibility for the child, which is a valid personal boundary.

I also consider the family dynamics. The user feels pressured by the family to help, but she has the right to make her own decisions. It's important to balance family expectations with personal comfort and responsibility.

In the end, while her decision might affect her cousin's custody case, it's her right to set boundaries. She's not obligated to compromise her comfort for others, especially when it comes to taking care of someone else's child. Therefore, her action might be seen as morally acceptable because it respects her personal boundaries and responsibilities.
